title: Write a JSON parser
summary: JSON.parse, by hand and from nothing. Turn the text into tokens, turn the tokens into values, nest to any depth, and get the escape and number rules right. A document that is not JSON has to throw rather than come back wrong.

checkpoints.title: The text becomes a token stream
checkpoints.hint: Strings and numbers are the two types you have to scan for: read forward from the character that opened them and return where you stopped, so the loop knows where to pick up. A token carries the JavaScript value, so the text -3.5 arrives as the number -3.5.

checkpoints.title: A flat document parses to the right value
checkpoints.hint: parseValue has already consumed the token it switched on, so parseObject starts after the opening brace and finishes by consuming the closing one. Empty is the case that bites: {} and [] never reach the comma loop at all.

checkpoints.title: Nesting goes as deep as the document does
checkpoints.hint: Depth comes free once parseObject and parseArray call parseValue for each member, because a member is a value and a value can be another object or array. Nothing here needs a depth counter.

checkpoints.title: Escapes, number edge cases, and refusing what is not JSON
checkpoints.hint: The tokeniser resolves escapes, so \n arrives as one newline character and \uXXXX as one character built from four hex digits. For the refusals, check that every token got consumed: 01 and {} junk both parse fine if you stop at the first value.

checkpoints.title: It agrees with JSON.parse on documents nobody wrote
checkpoints.hint: The failure prints the shortest document that disagrees, which is a complete test case. If JSON.parse refused it and you came back with a value, something was left over after the value ended. If you both came back with values, the difference is in a string escape or in a number the tokeniser read too eagerly.
